items.title: Here’s why last year’s government shutdown will haunt October’s inflation data.
items.full_text: The artificial intelligence boom has powered the U.S. economy through a period of tariffs, war and uncertainty. It has also pushed up prices, raised borrowing costs and set off fears of a financial bubble that could burst to devastating effect. Americans made clear in last week’s midterm elections that they do not think the trade-off has been worth it. Economists broadly expect a reprieve in October, with overall prices as measured by the Consumer Price Index rising 0.3 percent for the month after a 0.6 percent jump in September. “Core” prices, which strip out volatile food and energy items, are forecast to have risen just 0.2 percent. But don’t expect a year-over-year comparison. The agency will not release one given that it was unable to collect data during last year’s government shutdown, which ran from Oct. 1 through Nov. 12. The trajectory of inflation is being closely watched by the Federal Reserve. Tuesday’s C.P.I. report will be the last before the central bank meets for its final gathering of the year on Dec. 8 and 9. November’s report comes out the day after the meeting. Policymakers have broadly signaled that they will raise rates next month as they seek to stamp out price pressures that have pushed inflation further away from their goal. While the Fed closely tracks the C.P.I. report, it officially targets 2 percent inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index. That level has been overshot for nearly six years. Even as price pressures have intensified in recent months, officials have adopted a gradual approach to raising rates. They lifted borrowing costs by a quarter of a percentage point in September and then voted late last month to hold rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. That meeting came just days before the midterms. When asked whether the elections factored into the central bank’s decision-making, Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, said that “politics played no role in the decision.” How quickly the Fed raises rates going forward will depend largely on the incoming inflation data. The labor market remains in solid shape , as October’s report released on Friday affirmed. If price pressures begin to pick up again — or show signs of broadening out — that might necessitate the Fed raising rates at a faster clip , or perhaps having to do more over time to ensure that there is enough restraint on economic activity. Blame last fall’s federal government shutdown, which forced the Bureau of Labor Statistics to stop collecting price data for more than a month. As a result, the agency never released a price index for last October and can’t calculate a year-over-year change for today’s report. (The agency was able to collect data for a few products retroactively, and will be able to publish year-over-year changes for those items.) Many economists will estimate the 12-month change by taking an average of the September and November price levels and comparing the latest data to that. The New York Times will do the same in our coverage. (To be precise, we will be estimating the October 2025 price level by taking the geometric mean of the September and November numbers.) That approach may slightly overstate inflation over the past year. The C.P.I. for last November was artificially depressed because of quirks in the way government statisticians accounted for the missing data from the prior month. That will make the change in prices between this fall and last look larger than it otherwise would be. The uncertainty about the 12-month figure probably won’t matter much to officials at the Federal Reserve, who tend to focus on shorter-run changes for hints about where inflation is headed. And none of the methodological oddities will change the big picture, which is that inflation remains uncomfortably high. Voters overwhelmingly supported ballot initiatives that aimed to rein in data center development, and they elected to office governors and legislators who promised to do the same. Now the question for newly empowered Democrats, and for policymakers more broadly, is whether they can find a way to address voters’ concerns without derailing the economy. Many economists are optimistic, arguing that slowing the frenetic pace of the A.I. build out could make it more sustainable, even if it causes some short-term hardship. Some of the A.I. skeptics who won office last week, including Gina Hinojosa, the newly elected Democratic governor of Texas, have said they want to ensure data center projects benefit their communities, not stop them entirely. But the whipsawing of financial markets in the days after the 2026 election shows just how narrow a tightrope that is to walk. The mere suggestion of scrutiny in Washington has rattled both Silicon Valley and Wall Street, which enjoyed two years of lax regulation under Republicans’ watch. That tension was evident again on Monday, when Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the A.I. ecosystem, descended into a maelstrom over its chief executive’s relationship with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe to be a Chinese spy. President Trump came to his defense, some in Congress have called for investigations and Nvidia’s share price fell sharply Monday morning. The incident offered fresh evidence that the economy has become so dependent on A.I., and so much money has flooded into the sector, that deflating the bubble without popping it could prove difficult. Investors have made their bets on the assumption that the sector’s breakneck growth rate would continue for years, meaning that the market could be vulnerable if the pace slows even modestly. “It’s not like you can scientifically calibrate this dial,” said Jared Bernstein, who served as a top economic adviser to President Joseph R. Biden Jr. “The likelihood that things deflate in some sort of orderly way are low.” Powering Growth, Pushing Up Prices Voters elected governors and legislators to halt data center development. Credit... Aubrey Trinnaman for The New York Times The challenge for Democrats is that A.I. — and the building boom that developing it requires — has become embedded into nearly every aspect of the U.S. economy . Investors have pumped hundreds of billions of dollars of capital into companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, which have spent that money on microchips, data centers and the electricity to power them. The investments have filtered through the economy, lifting demand for steel, construction equipment and even the specialized gray paint used to coat the walls of data centers. At the same time, the rising share prices of A.I.-related companies have helped swell Americans’ brokerage accounts and retirement portfolios, helping to prop up consumer spending when rising prices and slowing wage growth are taking a toll on many people’s finances. Suppliers to the data centers have continued to add jobs even as the rest of the manufacturing industry has cut workers, according to an analysis by Devesh Kodnani, a fellow at the Economic Security Project, a progressive research organization. The story is similar in construction, where data center projects have helped make up for soft demand in housing, warehouses and office buildings. But while the boom has helped keep growth on track, it has also soaked up resources from other sectors. Companies found themselves forced to pay more for materials and labor. Shortages of memory chips led to higher prices for consumer electronics. The A.I. industry’s demand for power drove up electricity prices, while its demand for capital pushed up interest rates. “It’s almost as if corporate America has been so obsessed with this technology investment that it’s chosen to do so at the expense of other aspects of the economy,” said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING, an investment bank. That sense of corporate impunity helps explain public opposition to data centers, and to A.I. more generally, said Asad Ramzanali, director of A.I. and technology policy at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, a research institute at Vanderbilt University. Communities experience the costs of A.I. as noise, traffic and higher electricity bills, and even people who live nowhere near data centers worry about the effects that A.I. could have on their jobs, the climate or even the future of the human race. The benefits, on the other hand, seem mostly to be flowing to a relative handful of tech billionaires. “They see all the costs, they feel all the cost, they bear all the cost, and the benefits are not accruing in a meaningful way,” Mr. Ramzanali said. Policy Choices Representative Ted Lieu of California, a chair of a Democratic commission established in 2025 to study A.I.’s economic implications. Credit... Kenny Holston/The New York Times President Trump and his aides have shrugged off such criticisms, celebrating the potential riches to come from A.I. and the data centers that power the technology. The administration has also worked to ward off anything that might inhibit the development of those computing facilities — and their contribution to the economy’s growth. “As President, I am 100 percent in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them,” Mr. Trump said on social media, referring to data centers. “They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say ‘NO’ to the riches they bring!” Within days of the midterm election, some Democrats quickly pledged that they would use their newfound political strength to regulate A.I. and curtail data center construction. “One of the reasons the American people rose up against A.I. data centers is that they saw the A.I. industry was running wild, and the Trump administration was encouraging the A.I. industry to run wild,” said Representative Ted Lieu of California, a chair of a Democratic commission established in 2025 to study A.I.’s economic implications.
